meta.tagline: The Renaissance was born here — and the city reminds you of this on every corner, without ever becoming tiresome

pills: Visit museums early in the morning

overview.intro: Florence is a small city — the historic centre is compact enough to walk. Inside it: Botticelli, Michelangelo, Leonardo, Brunelleschi; the Uffizi, Accademia, Bargello; a church on every corner, a fresco in every church. The only way to deal with this density is to set priorities: if you try to see everything at once, you won't really see any of it. Florence's dusty stone buildings, narrow streets, morning markets and evening aperitivo come together in a formula found nowhere else. The Arno River divides the city in two; on the far bank, the Oltrarno neighbourhoods — where most tourists don't cross, where workshops and local bars carry on, where the real Florence lives.

local_word.definition: The poor man's kitchen. Florence's best dishes came from here: lampredotto (beef tripe), ribollita (stale bread soup), pappa al pomodoro (tomato and bread porridge). Cheap ingredients, long cooking times, deep flavour. Bistecca alla Fiorentina is expensive and showy — cucina povera is the real face of the city.

rules.title: Don't go to the Uffizi without a reservation
rules.description: The Uffizi and the Accademia (Michelangelo's David) are Florence's most visited museums. Queues at the door can last hours — you might not get in at all. Book tickets in advance from the official websites — there's a booking fee but it's worth every minute saved in the queue. The first hours of the morning (9-10am) are the least crowded.

rules.title: Tuscan bread is unsalted — be ready for this
rules.description: Pane sciocco (unsalted bread) is a centuries-old Tuscan tradition. It might seem strange on the first bite. But dipped into cured meats, cheese or sauces it makes sense — it's designed to absorb the salt from the food beside it, not to be eaten on its own. Schiacciata, however — the flat bread with olive oil and salt — is salty and delicious.

rules.title: Know what real gelato looks like
rules.description: High-piled gelato in big windows, neon coloured, is a tourist trap. Real good gelato looks the opposite: simple, understated, naturally coloured. Pistachio is yellowish not green, strawberry is pinkish not red. Because there's no colouring — the colour comes only from the natural ingredients.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: T2 tram to Santa Maria Novella ~25 min · €1.70

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: Single fare €1.70 · 90 minutes valid · buy at a tabacchi

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: Apr–May and Sep–Oct ideal · Jun–Aug very hot · Dec–Feb cold

tip.label: Piazzale Michelangelo — go for sunset but go early
tip.text: Florence's most famous viewpoint. The Duomo, Ponte Vecchio and the whole city spread out panoramically. Go 45 minutes before sunset to find yourself a good spot. You can walk up (about 20 minutes from Ponte Vecchio) or take bus number 13. Entry is free.

overview.title: Welcome to Florence

transport.intro: Florence is small and the historic centre is walkable. Bus and tram are the second option; taxis are expensive.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: The T2 Vespucci tram takes you from the airport to Santa Maria Novella train station in about 25 minutes. Departures every 5 minutes, ticket €1.70. From February 2025 the line was extended to Piazza San Marco. Fixed-price taxi around €22-25. The tram is easily the most practical option.

items.title: Autolinee Toscane — bus network
items.description: City buses and trams run on the same ticket system. Single fare €1.70, valid for 90 minutes, free transfers. Tickets available at tabacchi (tobacconist) shops, machines at bus stops or tram stops. You can't buy a ticket after boarding a bus — buy in advance and validate it when you get on. Contactless bank card payment of €1.70 is also accepted.

items.title: Tram — T1 and T2
items.description: Line T1 runs from Scandicci to Santa Maria Novella; line T2 runs from Vespucci Airport via Santa Maria Novella to Piazza San Marco. Both are useful for reaching the city centre. Same ticket as the bus, €1.70.

items.title: Bike and scooter
items.description: Florence's historic centre is largely pedestrianised — vehicles are restricted. Bike rental is available but take care on the narrow and busy streets. The route along the Arno is bike-friendly.

items.title: Walking — the best option
items.description: From the Duomo: Uffizi 10 minutes, Ponte Vecchio 15 minutes, Santa Croce 15 minutes, Mercato Centrale 10 minutes. The historic centre is almost entirely walkable. To cross to Oltrarno: 5 minutes on foot over Ponte Vecchio.

callout.label: ZTL — don't drive into the historic centre
callout.text: Florence's historic centre is a ZTL zone (Zona a Traffico Limitato) — restricted to vehicle traffic. Unauthorised vehicles are detected by automatic cameras and face heavy fines. If you've arrived by rental car, don't enter the historic centre. The best solution is to park outside and walk or use public transport.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Location matters in Florence — the historic centre is close to everything but expensive; Oltrarno is more local and better value.

local_word.definition: The other side of the Arno. Cross Ponte Vecchio and Oltrarno begins. Most tourists skip this bank — except those coming for the Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens. Workshops, small restaurants, neighbourhood bars and artist studios are on this side. Florence's quieter, more lived-in face.

items.name: Centro Storico — Historic Centre
items.description: The Duomo, Uffizi, Ponte Vecchio, Mercato Centrale all within walking distance. The closest point to everything, but also the busiest and most expensive. Streets are relatively quieter in the early morning and late evening.

items.name: Oltrarno
items.description: On the far side of Ponte Vecchio. The Pitti Palace, Boboli Gardens and Bardini Gardens are on this side. Piazza Santo Spirito fills up in the evenings. Workshops, boutique restaurants and neighbourhood bars here. 10-15 minutes on foot to the historic centre. Prices slightly better, atmosphere much more local.

items.name: Santa Croce neighbourhood
items.description: Around the Santa Croce Basilica. On the eastern side of the historic centre, 15 minutes on foot to the Uffizi. Tourist pressure slightly less than the centre. Sant'Ambrogio Market is in this neighbourhood — where locals do their morning shopping.

items.name: San Lorenzo neighbourhood
items.description: Around the Mercato Centrale and San Lorenzo Market. The liveliest neighbourhood in the mornings. The Medici Chapels and Laurentian Library are here. Market stalls and local cafés are active in the early part of the day.

items.name: Near Santa Maria Novella
items.description: Walking distance to Florence's main station, SMN. The airport tram (T2) passes through here. Practical for day trips around Tuscany — Siena, San Gimignano close to the train. Ten minutes on foot to the historic centre.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Florence can be visited year-round but summer crowds and heat reach their peak in July and August.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April and May are Florence's most balanced period. The weather is mild, tourists are around but far from summer levels. The wisteria at Bardini Gardens is in full bloom from mid-April to early May.

callout.label: Bardini Gardens wisteria — mid-April
callout.text: In Oltrarno, next to Forte di Belvedere. The long purple wisteria tunnels open from mid-April to early May. Much quieter than Boboli. The panorama of Florence from the top is free; entry to the garden is ticketed. Least crowded in the early morning hours.

items.subtitle: Spring · Wisteria, mild weather, manageable crowds

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot and crowded
items.description: July and August are the busiest and hottest months — 35-38°C is normal. Museums, bridges and squares are full of tourists. Without reservations you may not get into anything. Before 8am and after 8pm the city is relatively quiet. The evening aperitivo culture and bars along the Arno are at their liveliest this season.

callout.label: Estate Fiesolana — open-air events all summer
callout.text: In the hilltop town of Fiesole just above Florence, concerts, theatre and film screenings run all summer. Listening to music in an ancient Roman theatre is a different kind of experience. 30 minutes from Florence on bus number 7.

items.subtitle: Summer · Above 35°C, museums packed

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October see the crowds thin out while the weather stays mild. The grape harvest in the Chianti region begins in September-October. Trattorias open with new seasonal menus: mushrooms, game, chestnuts. Rain increases from November but museums are nearly empty.

callout.label: Chianti region — autumn's best escape
callout.text: Just south of Florence, 30-45 minutes by car. Greve in Chianti, Radda, Gaiole — small towns, wine cellars, olive groves. September-October is harvest time: many estates open to visitors for wine tasting. Bus services run from Florence without a car. Plan a full day.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Crowds thinning, wine harvest begins

items.label: Winter
items.name: Empty museums, quiet city
items.description: Christmas markets and lights bring the city to life in December. January and February are Florence's quietest period — museums nearly empty, no Uffizi queue, trattorias accessible without reservations. Cold but snow is rare. Late February brings Carnevale season.

callout.label: Schiacciata alla Fiorentina — the Carnival cake
callout.text: A soft sponge cake unique to Florence, flavoured with orange zest and dusted with icing sugar — with Florence's lily crest (giglio) pressed into the top. Available in bakeries and pastry shops during Carnevale (late January-February). Can be found year-round in some places but freshest and most widely available in this period.

items.subtitle: Winter · Least crowded, cheapest prices

monthly_highlights.text: Scoppio del Carro: the 'explosion of the cart' before the Duomo — a historic cart of fireworks lit by a mechanical dove, the same ritual for centuries.
San Giovanni: the patron saint's day — the calcio storico final (historic-costume rugby-meets-wrestling) and fireworks over the Arno at night.
Harvest: the Chianti hills bustle with the vendemmia; new wine in the city, and half-day vineyard trips at their loveliest.
The quiet season: short queues, cheap hotels, trattorias left to the locals — this is exactly ribollita season.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: Florence is home to one of Italy's finest cuisines — but without pretension. Bistecca is expensive, lampredotto is cheap; both are Florentine.

local_word.definition: A giant T-bone steak cut from Chianina breed cattle. At least 1.5 kilos, cooked over charcoal, served pink-red inside — ask for it well-done and they'll ask you to go somewhere else. Served only with olive oil, rock salt and fresh pepper. Sold by the kilo, expensive, eaten shared. Eating one in Florence at least once is non-negotiable.

items.name: Bistecca alla Fiorentina
items.description: Giant T-bone steak, Chianina beef, cooked over charcoal, red inside. €45-60 per kilo — shared between two people. It has to be 'al sangue' (rare). If you can accept that, this is one of Florence's most iconic experiences.
items.tag: €45–60 per kilo · for two · served rare

items.name: Lampredotto sandwich
items.description: The fourth stomach of the cow, boiled, sliced and placed into a simple semmel roll. Topped with salsa verde and chilli sauce. Ask for it 'bagnato' — they dip the top of the bread in the cooking broth, and the bread gets soaked — this is the critical difference. €4-5. At stalls in Mercato Centrale or Sant'Ambrogio Market. You'll either love it or not, but you can't leave Florence without trying.
items.tag: Mercato Centrale or Sant'Ambrogio · €4–5 · ask for 'bagnato'

items.name: Ribollita
items.description: A thick soup of white beans, cavolo nero (black kale), carrot, celery and stale Tuscan bread. The name means 'reboiled' because it's better the next day. A winter dish — October to March. Appears as a daily special at trattorias. Cheap and filling: €8-12.
items.tag: Winter months · daily special at trattorias · €8–12

items.name: Schiacciata sandwich
items.description: Tuscany's flat olive oil and salt bread (schiacciata), filled with prosciutto, pecorino or grilled vegetables. Florence's lunch-break food: quick, affordable, eaten standing. Fresh from bakeries from the morning onwards.

items.name: Real gelato
items.description: Metal containers, flat tops, natural colours: pistachio is yellowish-brown, strawberry pale pink. Those are real. Plastic containers, neon colours, high piled mounds — tourist trap. Gelateria dei Neri, Gelateria della Passera (Oltrarno), Bonchi.
items.tag: Gelateria dei Neri or Oltrarno options · €1.50–2.50 per scoop

items.name: Aperitivo culture
items.description: Between 6pm and 8pm. Order a Negroni or Aperol Spritz — small snacks come alongside. Some bars include a buffet with aperitivo. Oltrarno bars, Piazza Santo Spirito and Via San Niccolò are the right addresses for this ritual.
items.tag: 6–8pm · Oltrarno and Santo Spirito · Negroni or Spritz

callout.label: Mercato Centrale — best in the early morning
callout.text: Right next to San Lorenzo, a two-storey iron and glass building. Ground floor is the food market: butcher, fishmonger, cheesemonger, greengrocer — from 7am until early afternoon. Upstairs you can find pasta, pizza, lampredotto, bistecca at various stalls. Touristy but worth experiencing. The ground floor is local and real. Go down to the ground floor in the early morning and enjoy it. Head upstairs when you need a break.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Florence's quietest and most unexpected corners are usually overshadowed by the famous museums.

items.name: Bargello Museum
items.description: On Via del Proconsolo, 5 minutes' walk from the Uffizi. The most important collection of Renaissance sculpture is here: Donatello's David, Michelangelo's early works, Ghiberti and Verrocchio. A fraction of the Uffizi's visitor numbers. The first-floor courtyard — when afternoon light passes through it — is one of Florence's most beautiful and most silent spaces. Opens at 8:30am and is usually quiet until midday.
items.rarity: An escape from Uffizi crowds — the silence of the Bargello

items.name: Laurentian Library
items.description: On the upper floor of San Lorenzo Basilica, with a separate ticket. The entrance vestibule and its dramatic, wavy staircase designed by Michelangelo — one of the earliest examples of Mannerism. Around 11,000 Medici manuscripts are held here. Open Monday-Saturday 10am-1pm.

items.name: Caffetteria delle Oblate
items.description: On Via dell'Oriuolo, 3 minutes' walk from the Duomo. A small café on the rooftop of the city library. The rear façade of the Duomo and a city panorama in front of you with your coffee or aperitivo. Limited seating — check before you go. The library itself is free to enter — you can sit inside too.
items.rarity: A better Duomo view than any café — and a library

items.name: Piazza Santo Spirito
items.description: In Oltrarno, 15 minutes' walk from Ponte Vecchio. Quiet during the day — but after 6pm Florentines gather here. Bars and osterias all around, a fountain in the centre, people sitting on the steps. A small market runs every morning except Monday. Sunday brings an organic and craft market.

items.name: San Miniato al Monte
items.description: Just above Piazzale Michelangelo, 10 more minutes of walking. An 11th-century basilica above the city. A fraction of Piazzale's visitor numbers. The Tuscan marble floor and apse mosaic inside are among Florence's least-known art treasures. Go before sunset: first San Miniato, then down to Piazzale. Both are free.
items.rarity: The closest and least crowded view of Brunelleschi's dome

items.name: Ponte Vecchio — early morning
items.description: Between 7:30 and 8:30am, before the jewellery shops open, the bridge is almost empty. At this hour you can stand on it, watch the Arno and see the Vasari Corridor passing above. Note the open gap in the middle of the bridge: left deliberately open for the bust and the view of the Arno.
items.rarity: The bridge over the Arno — before the shops open

callout.label: Sant'Ambrogio Market — alternative to Mercato Centrale
callout.text: In the Santa Croce neighbourhood, at Piazza Sant'Ambrogio. Smaller, less touristy, more local. Fresh vegetables, fruit, cheese, meat. Small trattoria stalls inside — lampredotto or daily special for lunch. Open 7am-2pm, closed Sundays. Much less crowded than Mercato Centrale and much more genuine.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Book Uffizi tickets in advance
items.sub: At uffizi.it. Door queues can last hours. Choose the first entry at 9am — least crowded time.

items.label: Try a lampredotto sandwich
items.sub: Mercato Centrale or Sant'Ambrogio Market. €4-5. Ask for 'bagnato' — top of the bread dipped in broth. Eat standing.

items.label: Cross to Oltrarno
items.sub: Walk over Ponte Vecchio. Sit in Piazza Santo Spirito. Most alive after 6pm.

items.label: Visit the Bargello Museum
items.sub: Via del Proconsolo. 5 minutes from the Uffizi. Donatello's David is here. Usually queue-free.

items.label: Find real gelato
items.sub: Metal containers, natural colours, flat or slightly concave top. Gelateria dei Neri or Oltrarno options. €1.50-2.50 per scoop.

items.label: Go to Piazzale Michelangelo at sunset
items.sub: Arrive 45 minutes early. Bus 13 or 20-minute walk from Ponte Vecchio. Free entry.

items.label: Climb to San Miniato al Monte
items.sub: Just above Piazzale Michelangelo, 10 more minutes. 11th-century basilica. Free. Much quieter than Piazzale.

items.label: Do aperitivo — in Oltrarno
items.sub: 6-8pm. Santo Spirito or Via San Niccolò. Negroni or Spritz. Snacks come alongside.

items.label: Go to Mercato Centrale early in the morning
items.sub: Ground floor — food market. From 7am. Upstairs is touristy; ground floor is local and real.

items.label: Cross Ponte Vecchio early morning
items.sub: 7:30-8:30am with shops closed. Bridge nearly empty. Arno views and Vasari Corridor visible.

items.label: Try a schiacciata sandwich
items.sub: Any bakery. Flat olive oil bread, filled with prosciutto or cheese. €4-7. Lunch-break food.

items.label: Share a bistecca
items.sub: Minimum two people. €45-60 per kilo. 'Al sangue' — it will be served rare. Trattoria Mario or similar.

checklist.title: Florence Checklist
checklist.completion_message: You saw Florence with your eyes, not from a list.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Florence is small and tourist-dense; its traps are just as frequent. Know these four and tour the Renaissance in peace.

items.name: Street sellers of 'no-queue Uffizi'
items.description: The 'skip-the-line' hawkers around the museum charge multiples of the official ticket; some tickets turn out invalid at the door.
items.instead: Buy only from the official site, dated and timed; the calmest hours are the first slot and two hours before closing.

items.name: 'Real leather' on the San Lorenzo stalls
items.description: Not everything labelled 'vera pelle' is genuine; glued soles and synthetic leather abound on the tourist stalls.
items.instead: No flame test needed: check the stitching and the smell, and buy from workshops like the Scuola del Cuoio or long-established shops.

items.name: 'Fixed-price bistecca' on a photo menu
items.description: Real bistecca alla fiorentina is sold by the etto (100 g) and served rare; the promise of bistecca 'per plate' is a thinned-out disappointment.
items.instead: Go where the price is quoted per etto and accept it rare; sharing one between two is the tradition itself.

items.name: Reaching Piazzale Michelangelo at bus o'clock
items.description: Half an hour before sunset the terrace fills with coach convoys; the view is lovely, the experience a scrum.
items.instead: Climb ten minutes more: the steps of San Miniato al Monte give the same view plus monks' chanting — and room to breathe.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Cross the river in Florence: in the Oltrarno prices drop, craft is real, and Florentines sit at the tables. The tourist centre is the shop window; the city is in the workshop.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: The dome, David and an Oltrarno evening

steps.title: Climb the Duomo dome
steps.description: Reserve the first slot weeks ahead: 463 steps, Brunelleschi's miracle, and a view earned before breakfast.

steps.title: The Uffizi — selectively
steps.description: Botticelli, Leonardo, Caravaggio: target three rooms and leave in two hours. Those who try to see everything see nothing.

steps.title: Lampredotto break
steps.description: Lampredotto from Nerbone or a street cart: Florence's working-class classic; courage rewarded with flavour.

steps.title: Ponte Vecchio + Oltrarno workshops
steps.description: Cross the bridge, from the goldsmiths' windows into the craft streets: bookbinders, carpenters, restorers.

steps.title: San Miniato sunset
steps.description: Climb to the thousand-year basilica above the Piazzale; as the city burns gold, the monks begin their chant.

steps.title: Santo Spirito evening
steps.description: Aperitivo on the square, then bistecca or ribollita: tables on the street, life on the piazza.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The icons
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: dome, Uffizi, Oltrarno, San Miniato.

steps.title: David and the Medici
steps.description: David at the Accademia in the morning (first slot), then Michelangelo's staircase at the Laurentian Library, the Bargello courtyard in the afternoon, a trattoria around San Lorenzo at night.

steps.title: Slow Florence and goodbye
steps.description: The Boboli or Bardini gardens in the morning, lunch with locals at the Sant'Ambrogio market, coffee with a dome view on the Oblate terrace, and one last gelato — the real kind.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: The Italian courtesy trio plus two Florentine touches; these five open every door.

items.meaning: Good morning / good day — mandatory when entering a shop
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — Chianti glasses rise to this
How beautiful! — the sentence you'll need ten times a day in Florence
